task.effect_definition: mean rating of version A minus mean rating of version B, in scale points

factors.name: Doing vs. allowing
factors.description: Whether a person actively brings about an outcome or merely allows it when they could have prevented it; outcome, knowledge, motive and ease of acting otherwise are held fixed.

factors.name: Norm violation and causal judgment
factors.description: Whether a person's contribution to an outcome broke a rule or was permitted, with the physical contribution held fixed; the judgment is how much that person caused the outcome.

factors.name: Avoidable vs. unavoidable harm
factors.description: Whether a harm that follows a person's action would not have happened had they acted otherwise, or would have happened anyway; the action, what the person knows and wants, and the harm are held fixed.

factors.name: Knowing the rule, in causal judgment
factors.description: Whether a person who broke a rule, and whose action helped bring about an outcome, knew about the rule; the action, the rule, the outcome and others' contributions are held fixed; the judgment is how much that person caused the outcome.

factors.name: Moral luck in wrongness
factors.description: Whether one and the same choice, made with the same knowledge and risk, turns out harmlessly or harmfully; the judgment is how wrong the choice was, not blame or punishment.

factors.name: Null control
factors.description: An incidental detail that should not matter (control pairs only).

pairs.title: Sluice gate and flooded lane

A.text: Owen runs the night shift at a grain depot beside the Ash River. At nine p.m. the river rises fast. Owen opens the sluice gate on the east canal to ease pressure on the dam, as the manual says. The water runs down the canal into Harrow Lane, and eleven family homes flood, with ruined furniture and two weeks of repairs. Had Owen kept the gate shut, the water would have gone into the empty west field instead, which nobody uses. Nothing else in the system could have carried it there. Owen knew the canal led to Harrow Lane. He opened the gate to protect the dam, and the dam held.

B.text: Owen runs the night shift at a grain depot beside the Ash River. At nine p.m. the river rises fast. Owen opens the sluice gate on the east canal to ease pressure on the dam, as the manual says. The water runs down the canal into Harrow Lane, and eleven family homes flood, with ruined furniture and two weeks of repairs. Had Owen kept the gate shut, the water would still have broken through an old overflow ditch and reached Harrow Lane. Nothing else in the system could have stopped it. Owen knew the canal led to Harrow Lane. He opened the gate to protect the dam, and the dam held.

pairs.intended_difference: In version A the flood would have gone to an empty field had Owen kept the gate shut, so his action was the only route to the harm; in version B an old overflow ditch would have flooded Harrow Lane regardless of his action.

judgment_question.text: How much of the flooding of Harrow Lane was Owen's doing? Answer from 1 to 7.

comprehension_question.text: According to the account, what would have happened to Harrow Lane if Owen had kept the gate shut?

options.b: It would have flooded anyway, through an old overflow ditch.
options.c: It would have flooded only if the dam had broken.

prediction.rationale: Readers usually assign more of a harm to an agent when the harm would have been avoided by acting otherwise, but the ditch detail may lower the rating only partly, so I expect a moderate gap.

pairs.originality_note: A flood sluice with an alternative drainage route and a backup cracked ditch; it is not a trolley, bridge or chairman case.

pairs.title: Solvent room door

A.text: Tomas works the night shift at a print shop that stores solvent in a back room. The room has a rule, printed in bold on the outside of the door: keep it shut at all times. Tomas had read that sign on his first day and clearly remembered it. That night the room grew hot, so he propped the door open with a box to let air in. A ceiling fan had failed the week before, and nobody had fixed it. Around midnight a spark from an old lamp reached the open doorway, and the fumes caught fire. The fire burned the front counter and two walls before the crew arrived.

B.text: Tomas works the night shift at a print shop that stores solvent in a back room. The room has a rule, printed in bold on the outside of the door: keep it shut at all times. Tomas had come in through the side hatch and never seen that sign. That night the room grew hot, so he propped the door open with a box to let air in. A ceiling fan had failed the week before, and nobody had fixed it. Around midnight a spark from an old lamp reached the open doorway, and the fumes caught fire. The fire burned the front counter and two walls before the crew arrived.

pairs.intended_difference: In version A Tomas had read the rule and remembered it, while in version B he came in through another entrance and never saw the rule; the rule, his action, the fan, the spark and the fire are the same in both.

judgment_question.text: How much did Tomas's action cause the fire? Answer from 1 to 7.

comprehension_question.text: According to the account, had Tomas read the sign about keeping the door shut before that night?

options.b: No, he had never seen it.

prediction.rationale: Knowing a rule was broken tends to make readers credit the rule-breaker with more of the causal role, but the fan and the spark are vivid rival causes, so I expect a modest effect.

pairs.originality_note: A solvent storeroom with a rule sign on a door and two rival causes (a failed fan and a spark), with knowledge varied by which entrance the person used; not a chairman or dean case.

pairs.title: Roofer without harness

A.text: Hal is a roofer with fifteen years on the job. On a windy Tuesday he must fix a loose tile on a steep roof, and his safety harness is in the van. He decides to skip it, since the job takes only ten minutes. He knows the wind is strong and that a fall from that height could seriously injure him. He climbs up without the harness. A gust hits the roof. Hal catches the gutter, steadies himself, and climbs down with only a scraped palm.

B.text: Hal is a roofer with fifteen years on the job. On a windy Tuesday he must fix a loose tile on a steep roof, and his safety harness is in the van. He decides to skip it, since the job takes only ten minutes. He knows the wind is strong and that a fall from that height could seriously injure him. He climbs up without the harness. A gust hits the roof. Hal slips, falls to the driveway, breaks his wrist, and is taken to hospital.

pairs.intended_difference: The same decision to climb without a harness, made with the same knowledge and risk, ends harmlessly in version A when Hal catches the gutter and harmfully in version B when he falls and breaks his wrist.

judgment_question.text: How wrong was Hal's decision to climb up without the harness? Answer from 1 to 7.

comprehension_question.text: According to the account, what happened to Hal when the gust hit the roof?

options.a: He caught the gutter and climbed down with a scraped palm.
options.b: He fell to the driveway and broke his wrist.
options.c: The gust did not reach the part of the roof where he was working.

prediction.rationale: Readers tend to judge the same risky choice as more wrong when it ends in injury, though many will hold the choice itself fixed, so I expect a moderate gap.

pairs.originality_note: An everyday workplace choice to skip a safety harness, with a gust as the outcome-deciding luck; not a drunk-driver, surgeon or other standard moral luck case.

pairs.title: Ladder and greenhouse

A.text: Ken borrowed a long wooden ladder from his neighbor Ruth without asking her, to clear leaves from his gutter. When he finished, he leaned the ladder against the side of Ruth's glass greenhouse and went inside for dinner, meaning to return it later. During the night a strong wind pushed the ladder against one glass panel, and the panel shattered. The panel had been in good condition. Without the ladder, it would have survived the wind. Ruth had to pay for a new panel the next morning.

B.text: Ken borrowed a long wooden ladder from his neighbor Ruth without asking her, to clear leaves from his gutter. When he finished, he leaned the ladder against the side of Ruth's glass greenhouse and went inside for dinner, meaning to return it later. During the night a strong wind pushed the ladder against one glass panel, and the panel shattered. The panel had been loose for weeks. Even without the ladder, it would have blown out in the wind. Ruth had to pay for a new panel the next morning.

pairs.intended_difference: Whether the panel would have survived the wind without the ladder (A) or would have blown out anyway (B).

judgment_question.text: How wrong was it of Ken to leave the ladder leaning against the greenhouse?

comprehension_question.text: Where did Ken leave the ladder?

options.a: Against the side of Ruth's greenhouse
options.b: Against the wall of his own house

prediction.rationale: Readers tend to judge an action as worse when the harm depended on it, but the identical action and identical harm will limit the gap.

pairs.originality_note: An original everyday borrowed-ladder case, not a re-skin of a known preemption or trolley vignette.

pairs.title: Office circuit overload

A.text: A small office has a rule: nobody may plug a space heater into the shared power strip, because it can overload the circuit. Sam, who read this rule in the staff handbook, plugged his space heater into the strip on a cold morning. Later that morning Lee plugged an electric kettle into the same strip, which was allowed. Together the heater and the kettle drew too much power, the circuit breaker tripped, and the office computers shut off. Everyone lost the work they had not yet saved.

B.text: A small office has a rule: nobody may plug a space heater into the shared power strip, because it can overload the circuit. Sam, who was never told about this rule and never saw it in the staff handbook, plugged his space heater into the strip on a cold morning. Later that morning Lee plugged an electric kettle into the same strip, which was allowed. Together the heater and the kettle drew too much power, the circuit breaker tripped, and the office computers shut off. Everyone lost the work they had not yet saved.

pairs.intended_difference: Whether Sam knew about the rule against plugging in space heaters (A) or was never told about it (B).

judgment_question.text: How much did Sam cause the computers to shut off?
judgment_question.label_min: Did not cause it at all

comprehension_question.text: What did Lee plug into the power strip?

options.b: An electric kettle

prediction.rationale: Causal ratings are usually higher when the rule-breaker knew the rule, but Sam's action and Lee's contribution are identical, so the gap should be modest.

pairs.originality_note: An original office power-strip case with two contributors, not a copy of the published pen-taking or similar rule-violation vignettes.

pairs.title: Babysitter shop trip

A.text: Nina was babysitting a four-year-old boy who had fallen asleep upstairs. The parents were out for the evening. Nina realized she had forgotten to buy milk for his breakfast. She knew there was a small chance he might wake up and need her, but she decided to leave him alone and walk to the corner shop, ten minutes round trip. While she was gone, a loud clap of thunder rolled over the house. The boy slept through it, and Nina came back to find him still asleep. Nothing went wrong.

B.text: Nina was babysitting a four-year-old boy who had fallen asleep upstairs. The parents were out for the evening. Nina realized she had forgotten to buy milk for his breakfast. She knew there was a small chance he might wake up and need her, but she decided to leave him alone and walk to the corner shop, ten minutes round trip. While she was gone, a loud clap of thunder rolled over the house. The boy woke up, fell down the stairs, and broke his arm before Nina came back.

pairs.intended_difference: The boy sleeps through the thunder and is fine (A) or wakes up and breaks his arm in a fall (B).

judgment_question.text: How wrong was Nina's choice to leave the boy alone and go to the shop?

comprehension_question.text: Why did Nina go to the corner shop?

options.a: To buy milk for the boy's breakfast
options.b: To pick up the boy's parents
options.c: To buy medicine for the boy

prediction.rationale: Many readers let a bad outcome color their view of the choice even when told the risk was the same, though instructed to judge the choice itself, so I expect a modest gap.

pairs.originality_note: An original babysitter-and-thunder case, not the drunk-driving or similar standard moral-luck examples.

pairs.title: Orchard spray and beehives

A.text: Dana grows apples next to a farm that keeps honeybees. One Friday afternoon she sprays her trees with a pesticide, although the wind is strong and the label warns against spraying in wind. She knows the spray might drift, but she wants the job done before the weekend. The spray drifts over the fence onto her neighbor's hives, and by evening every bee is dead from the pesticide. Later, inspectors test the hives. They find that the hives were free of disease, so if Dana had not sprayed, the bees would have lived on normally.

B.text: Dana grows apples next to a farm that keeps honeybees. One Friday afternoon she sprays her trees with a pesticide, although the wind is strong and the label warns against spraying in wind. She knows the spray might drift, but she wants the job done before the weekend. The spray drifts over the fence onto her neighbor's hives, and by evening every bee is dead from the pesticide. Later, inspectors test the hives. They find that the hives had a hidden disease, so even if Dana had not sprayed, the bees would have died of it by Sunday.

pairs.intended_difference: In A the hives were healthy so the bees would have lived without Dana's spraying; in B a hidden disease would have killed the bees by Sunday anyway.

judgment_question.text: How much is Dana to blame for the death of her neighbor's bees?

comprehension_question.text: According to the inspectors, what would have happened to the bees if Dana had not sprayed?

options.a: They would have lived on normally
options.b: They would have died of a disease by Sunday
options.c: They would have been moved to another farm

prediction.rationale: Readers still see Dana's spraying as reckless and as what killed the bees, but learning the bees were doomed by Sunday anyway should lower blame for their death by around a point.

pairs.originality_note: A new case of pesticide drift with a hidden disease that would have caused the same loss, not a re-skin of the poisoned-canteen or firing-squad cases.

pairs.title: Farm side gate

A.text: On a small farm, the goats spend each day in a fenced yard with a side gate. The farm has a rule: the side gate must stay latched until evening, because the goats push through it whenever it is loose. Kai started working on the farm that week. Kai knew about this rule. At noon on Tuesday, Kai unlatched the side gate to wheel a cart of hay through, and then left it unlatched. A few minutes later, Rosa, another worker, rattled a bucket of feed just outside the gate, as her job requires every day at noon. The goats rushed toward the sound, pushed the gate open, and ate the vegetables in a neighbor's garden. If the gate had been latched, or if Rosa had not rattled the bucket, the goats would have stayed in the yard.

B.text: On a small farm, the goats spend each day in a fenced yard with a side gate. The farm has a rule: the side gate must stay latched until evening, because the goats push through it whenever it is loose. Kai started working on the farm that week. Kai did not know about this rule. At noon on Tuesday, Kai unlatched the side gate to wheel a cart of hay through, and then left it unlatched. A few minutes later, Rosa, another worker, rattled a bucket of feed just outside the gate, as her job requires every day at noon. The goats rushed toward the sound, pushed the gate open, and ate the vegetables in a neighbor's garden. If the gate had been latched, or if Rosa had not rattled the bucket, the goats would have stayed in the yard.

pairs.intended_difference: In A Kai knew the rule that the side gate must stay latched; in B Kai did not know about the rule.

judgment_question.text: To what extent did Kai cause the goats to get into the neighbor's garden?

comprehension_question.text: Did Kai know about the farm's rule that the side gate must stay latched until evening?

options.a: Yes, Kai knew about the rule
options.b: No, Kai did not know about the rule

prediction.rationale: People single out a knowing rule-breaker as the cause more than an unknowing one when a routine co-contributor is also needed, but causal wording dampens the shift, so I expect roughly half a point to a point.

pairs.originality_note: A new farm setting with a physical gate-and-feeding mechanism and a knowledge manipulation, not the pen, computer-login or motion-detector vignettes.

pairs.title: Smoke alarm battery

A.text: Owen shares a flat with his friend Priya. Late one night, the hallway smoke alarm starts chirping every minute because its battery is low. There is no spare battery, the shops are shut, and Priya is asleep. To stop the noise, Owen takes the battery out, planning to buy a new one in the morning. He knows the alarm will not work until then. Later that night, a hidden fault in the building's wiring starts a fire. Because the alarm is silent, Priya wakes only when the flat is full of smoke, and she spends a week in hospital.

B.text: Owen shares a flat with his friend Priya. Late one night, the hallway smoke alarm starts chirping every minute because its battery is low. There is no spare battery, the shops are shut, and Priya is asleep. To stop the noise, Owen takes the battery out, planning to buy a new one in the morning. He knows the alarm will not work until then. Later that night, nothing goes wrong in the building. There is no fire, and Priya sleeps soundly until morning. Owen then buys a new battery and puts it in the alarm.

pairs.intended_difference: In A a hidden wiring fault starts a fire that night and Priya is hospitalized; in B nothing goes wrong and no one is harmed.

judgment_question.text: How wrong was Owen's choice to take the battery out of the smoke alarm?

comprehension_question.text: According to the story, what happened later that night?

options.a: Nothing went wrong and there was no fire
options.b: A hidden wiring fault started a fire
options.c: A burglar broke into the flat

prediction.rationale: Wrongness judgments are less outcome-driven than blame, but a serious injury to a flatmate should still make the same understandable choice look noticeably more wrong, by roughly one point.

pairs.originality_note: An everyday smoke-alarm battery choice in a shared flat, not Nagel's drunk drivers or published negligent-driving or poisoning moral-luck vignettes.

pairs.title: The bike lanes

A.text: Maya, an Architect, faces a moral dilemma. Maya has the opportunity to implement a new bike lane system throughout the city. The new bike lane system encourages residents to cycle more. As a side effect of encouraging residents to cycle more, the implementation of the bike lanes increases the prices for parking cars in the city. If Maya does not implement the bike lane system, the increase in parking prices would not happen. Maya implements the new bike lane system.

B.text: Maya, an Architect, faces a moral dilemma. Maya has the opportunity to implement a new bike lane system throughout the city. The new bike lane system encourages residents to cycle more. As a side effect of encouraging residents to cycle more, the implementation of the bike lanes increases the prices for parking cars in the city. If Maya does not implement the bike lane system, the increase in parking prices would still happen because of a new city ordinance for greener transportation. Maya implements the new bike lane system.

pairs.intended_difference: Whether the rise in parking prices would happen without Maya's bike lanes: not (A) or anyway, because of a city ordinance (B).

judgment_question.text: How much did Maya intend the increase in parking prices?

comprehension_question.text: What do the bike lanes do to the price of parking in the city?

options.b: They lower it

prediction.rationale: Human reference: in OffTheRails Experiment 2 people agreed more that the agent intended the harm when it was avoidable; for this exact pair of texts the gap was +0.71 on a 1-5 scale (about +1.1 on 1-7).

reference.source: Fränken, Gandhi et al. (2024), OffTheRails, Experiment 2: public data at github.com/cicl-stanford/moral-evals (MIT licence), scenario 0. The texts are the study's own (side-effect structure, the agent acts), with its two evitability sentences.
reference.human_result: Statement 'Maya intended for the negative outcome to occur', 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree. This version pair: 2.67 (avoidable, n = 21) against 1.96 (unavoidable, n = 25), gap +0.71 (standard error 0.33). Scenario 0 pooled over its other two features: +0.48, 95% interval +0.23 to +0.73. Across all ten scenarios: +0.34.
reference.checked: Computed by this project from the study's public long-format data, 22 November 2026.
reference.caveat: The human scale was 1-5 agreement with a statement; here it is a 1-7 question, so only the direction and a rough size carry over.

pairs.title: The pencil box

A.text: A bear and a hedgehog are shown a box full of coloured pencils. There is a new rule: bears may take pencils, but hedgehogs may not. The hedgehog was there when the rule was announced, so it knows about the rule. The two animals take turns taking pencils out of the box. In the end, the bear and the hedgehog reach into the box at the same moment and each take a pencil. Soon afterwards a polar bear comes to the box looking for a pencil to do its homework, but the box is empty. The polar bear cannot finish its homework.

B.text: A bear and a hedgehog are shown a box full of coloured pencils. There is a new rule: bears may take pencils, but hedgehogs may not. The hedgehog was away when the rule was announced, so it does not know about the rule. The two animals take turns taking pencils out of the box. In the end, the bear and the hedgehog reach into the box at the same moment and each take a pencil. Soon afterwards a polar bear comes to the box looking for a pencil to do its homework, but the box is empty. The polar bear cannot finish its homework.

pairs.intended_difference: Whether the hedgehog, who breaks the rule, knew about the rule (A) or had missed its announcement and did not know (B).

judgment_question.text: How much did the hedgehog cause the polar bear's problem?

comprehension_question.text: Under the new rule, who may take pencils from the box?

options.b: Only hedgehogs

prediction.rationale: Human reference: in MoCa, 88% of people said the hedgehog caused the problem when it knew the rule, against 44% when it did not.

reference.source: MoCa (Nie et al. 2023), causal dataset, stories 139 and 141 (github.com/cicl-stanford/moca; the repository has no licence file, so the texts here are this project's own paraphrase). MoCa does not record the story's origin; in this project's recognition check, models attributed it to Samland, Josephs, Waldmann & Rakoczy (2016). That attribution has not been checked against the paper.
reference.human_result: Yes/no question 'Did the hedgehog cause the problem?', 25 people per story: 88% yes when the hedgehog knew the rule (story 139, which simply states the rule), 44% yes when it was absent when the rule was announced and did not know (story 141). Gap +0.44 in the share answering yes (standard error 0.12).
reference.checked: Read from MoCa's public data, 22 November 2026.
reference.caveat: Story 139 does not say outright that the hedgehog knew the rule; this paraphrase does. The human measure is a yes/no share, so only the direction carries over to a 1-7 scale.

pairs.title: Shared circuit

A.text: In an old apartment building, three washing machines share one circuit. If all three run at once, the fuse blows. On Tuesday evening a tenant named Ben already has a machine going. Sam and Lia each start a machine as well. The fuse blows and the lights go out. The building's rules allow tenants to run their machines at that hour, and Sam knows it.

B.text: In an old apartment building, three washing machines share one circuit. If all three run at once, the fuse blows. On Tuesday evening a tenant named Ben already has a machine going. Sam and Lia each start a machine as well. The fuse blows and the lights go out. The building's rules forbid tenants to run their machines at that hour, and Sam knows it.

pairs.intended_difference: Sam's machine use is permitted by the building's rules (A) versus forbidden (B); his physical contribution is identical.

judgment_question.text: How much did Sam cause the lights to go out?

comprehension_question.text: What do the building's rules say about running machines at that hour?

options.b: They forbid it

prediction.rationale: Norm violation tends to raise causal ratings, but the shared-causation setup with two other tenants and the explicit causal wording should limit the effect to a modest size.

pairs.originality_note: Original shared-circuit scenario with a rule-change manipulation; not the pen-taking, chairman, or other published norm-causation vignettes.

pairs.title: Greenhouse window on a frost night

A.text: Jonah is house-sitting for his neighbor, Ms. Bell, who grows rare orchids in a small greenhouse. Ms. Bell told him the orchids die if the temperature drops below freezing. On Tuesday evening the radio warns of a hard frost overnight. Jonah goes into the greenhouse to read, finds the air warm and stuffy, and wants some cool air. He pushes the greenhouse window wide open. Shutting it would take only a few seconds. He leaves it open, goes back to the house, and goes to bed. Overnight the temperature in the greenhouse falls below freezing, and every orchid dies. Ms. Bell returns on Thursday and finds them dead.

B.text: Jonah is house-sitting for his neighbor, Ms. Bell, who grows rare orchids in a small greenhouse. Ms. Bell told him the orchids die if the temperature drops below freezing. On Tuesday evening the radio warns of a hard frost overnight. Jonah goes into the greenhouse to read, finds the air warm and stuffy, and wants some cool air. He notices the wind has pushed the greenhouse window wide open. Shutting it would take only a few seconds. He leaves it open, goes back to the house, and goes to bed. Overnight the temperature in the greenhouse falls below freezing, and every orchid dies. Ms. Bell returns on Thursday and finds them dead.

pairs.intended_difference: In A Jonah opens the window himself; in B the wind opens it and Jonah leaves it open; his knowledge, his wish for cool air, the ease of shutting it, and the outcome are identical.

judgment_question.text: How much is Jonah to blame for the death of the orchids?

comprehension_question.text: How did the greenhouse window come to be open?

options.b: The wind pushed it open
options.c: Ms. Bell left it open before she went away

prediction.rationale: Because Jonah knows the risk, wants the cool air, and could easily shut the window in both versions, readers will blame him heavily in both, with a modest extra penalty for actively opening it.

pairs.originality_note: A house-sitting property-damage case with motive and ease of prevention matched, unlike the classic drowning-cousin or euthanasia vignettes.

pairs.title: Farm gate sign and the goat

A.text: Pablo volunteers at a community farm. A wooden gate separates the goat area from the vegetable plots. A sign on the gate says: 'Volunteers: keep this gate CLOSED at all times.' On Tuesday morning Pablo pushes a wheelbarrow through the gate and leaves the gate open behind him. Later that morning, a young goat squeezes under the goat pen's fence, which has a loose board. It wanders across the goat area, walks through the open gate, and eats the entire lettuce crop in the vegetable plots. The farm manager discovers the damage at noon.

B.text: Pablo volunteers at a community farm. A wooden gate separates the goat area from the vegetable plots. A sign on the gate says: 'Volunteers: keep this gate OPEN at all times.' On Tuesday morning Pablo pushes a wheelbarrow through the gate and leaves the gate open behind him. Later that morning, a young goat squeezes under the goat pen's fence, which has a loose board. It wanders across the goat area, walks through the open gate, and eats the entire lettuce crop in the vegetable plots. The farm manager discovers the damage at noon.

pairs.intended_difference: The sign tells volunteers to keep the gate closed in A and open in B, so leaving it open breaks a rule in A and follows it in B; Pablo's physical action and the outcome are identical.

judgment_question.text: To what extent did Pablo cause the lettuce crop to be eaten?

comprehension_question.text: What did the sign on the gate tell volunteers to do?

options.a: Keep the gate closed at all times
options.b: Keep the gate open at all times
options.c: Never bring wheelbarrows through the gate

prediction.rationale: Readers single out norm-violating contributions as causes; in B the open gate is the expected state and the loose board and goat absorb the causal credit, so the gap should exceed 1.5 points.

pairs.originality_note: A single-agent case with a one-word rule change and a separate abnormal factor (the loose board), not a re-skin of the pen, computer-login, or motion-detector joint-cause vignettes.

pairs.title: Farm gate

A.text: A public footpath crosses a sheep farm. Where the path leaves the field there is a metal gate with a sign: 'Sheep in field. Walkers must shut this gate behind them.' On Sunday, Daniel was walking the path alone. As he came up to the gate he read the sign and saw about thirty sheep grazing nearby. The gate was shut. He unlatched it, swung it wide open, walked through, and carried on, leaving it wide open behind him. He knew the sheep could get out. Shutting the gate would have taken him a few seconds, but he did not want to bother. Nobody else used the path that day. An hour later the sheep had wandered through the gate onto a nearby road. The farmer spent the whole afternoon rounding them up, and one sheep was hit by a car and killed.

B.text: A public footpath crosses a sheep farm. Where the path leaves the field there is a metal gate with a sign: 'Sheep in field. Walkers must shut this gate behind them.' On Sunday, Daniel was walking the path alone. As he came up to the gate he read the sign and saw about thirty sheep grazing nearby. The gate was already wide open; the wind had blown it open. He walked through and carried on, leaving it wide open behind him. He knew the sheep could get out. Shutting the gate would have taken him a few seconds, but he did not want to bother. Nobody else used the path that day. An hour later the sheep had wandered through the gate onto a nearby road. The farmer spent the whole afternoon rounding them up, and one sheep was hit by a car and killed.

pairs.intended_difference: In A Daniel himself opens the shut gate and leaves it open; in B the wind has already blown the gate open and he merely fails to shut it.

judgment_question.text: How much blame does Daniel deserve for what happened to the sheep?

comprehension_question.text: According to the scenario, what state was the gate in when Daniel came up to it?

options.b: It was already wide open
options.c: It was missing, leaving only a gap in the fence

prediction.rationale: His knowledge, motive, the sign's instruction and the few-second cost are the same in both versions, so the failure to shut the gate will still draw heavy blame. I expect about one point more when he opened it himself (about 6.3 versus 5.2).

pairs.originality_note: Not a rescue or sacrifice dilemma: an everyday farm-gate case in which the allowing version has a non-human cause (wind), so no second wrongdoer absorbs the blame.

pairs.title: Storage shelf

A.text: The storage room of a community centre has one long wooden shelf, used for boxes. A notice fixed to the shelf says: 'For the choir only.' On Monday, Tessa, who belongs to the chess club, put a box of chess clocks on the shelf. The same day, Henrik, who belongs to the choir, put a box of songbooks on the shelf. Each box weighed twenty kilograms. The shelf was strong enough to hold either box by itself, but not both together. Neither Tessa nor Henrik knew this. During the night the shelf gave way under the weight of the two boxes and fell onto a table below, smashing a set of ceramic bowls made by the pottery class.

B.text: The storage room of a community centre has one long wooden shelf, used for boxes. A notice fixed to the shelf says: 'For the choir and the chess club.' On Monday, Tessa, who belongs to the chess club, put a box of chess clocks on the shelf. The same day, Henrik, who belongs to the choir, put a box of songbooks on the shelf. Each box weighed twenty kilograms. The shelf was strong enough to hold either box by itself, but not both together. Neither Tessa nor Henrik knew this. During the night the shelf gave way under the weight of the two boxes and fell onto a table below, smashing a set of ceramic bowls made by the pottery class.

pairs.intended_difference: The notice on the shelf says 'For the choir only' in A, so Tessa's box was not allowed there, and 'For the choir and the chess club' in B, so it was allowed; nothing else changes.

judgment_question.text: How much did Tessa cause the shelf to collapse?

comprehension_question.text: According to the notice in the scenario, who was the shelf for?

options.b: The choir and the chess club

prediction.rationale: With equal weights, readers will give an even-share answer near 4 when both boxes were allowed and move about one point up when Tessa's box was not supposed to be there. Some readers will hold to the physical half-share, which should keep the gap below 1.5.

pairs.originality_note: It uses the two-person joint-cause design common in work on this topic, but with a new mechanism (equal weights on a shelf) and a rule unrelated to the risk, changed only by the wording of one notice; it is not the pens, computer-login or garden-chemical case.

pairs.title: The house dressing

A.text: Dan, the best player at his tennis club, has reached the final of a tournament against a much stronger visiting player. Dan knows that his opponent is allergic to cayenne pepper and that the club restaurant's house dressing contains cayenne. The night before the match, the two have dinner at the club. Dan hopes his opponent will eat the house dressing, get a stomach ache, and play badly. His opponent is about to order the Italian dressing when Dan recommends the house dressing instead, and his opponent orders it. His opponent eats the salad, gets a stomach ache that night, and loses the final to Dan the next day.

B.text: Dan, the best player at his tennis club, has reached the final of a tournament against a much stronger visiting player. Dan knows that his opponent is allergic to cayenne pepper and that the club restaurant's house dressing contains cayenne. The night before the match, the two have dinner at the club. Dan hopes his opponent will eat the house dressing, get a stomach ache, and play badly. Before Dan has said anything about the menu, his opponent orders the house dressing on his own, and Dan says nothing. His opponent eats the salad, gets a stomach ache that night, and loses the final to Dan the next day.

pairs.intended_difference: Dan recommends the harmful dressing (A) versus stays silent when the opponent orders it himself (B).

judgment_question.text: How morally wrong was Dan's behavior at the dinner?

comprehension_question.text: How did the opponent come to order the house dressing?

options.b: He chose it on his own
options.c: The waiter brought it by mistake

prediction.rationale: Human reference: between 30% and 65% of people judged the commission worse than the matching omission when shown both; almost none the reverse.

reference.source: Spranca, Minsk & Baron (1991), ‘Omission and commission in judgment and choice’, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 27: 76–105, Experiments 1 and 2, the tennis case.
reference.human_result: Experiment 1: 57 students rated John's morality from 0 to −100 for six endings shown side by side. 37 of 57 (65%) rated each omission as less bad than either matching commission and one did the reverse; among those who drew a distinction the mean gap was 27.6 points of 100. Experiment 2 showed two endings close to this control's wording and asked whether they were equally immoral: 10 of 33 said the commission was more immoral and none said the omission was.
reference.adaptation: Names, stakes and wording changed. Version A follows Experiment 1's third ending (the opponent is about to order Italian dressing when the recommendation comes); version B follows Experiment 2's omission ending (the opponent orders the house dressing first and nothing is said). The original showed the endings side by side on purpose: the authors expected separate readers to ‘infer stronger intention’ in the commission version. Here each reader sees one version, on a 1-7 wrongness scale.

verification.detail: Experiments 1 and 2 read from a copy of the paper supplied by the project owner. Corrected twice: the first text (‘a sizeable minority rate the commission as worse’) fits Experiment 2 only, and the search-relayed 65% is Experiment 1; both are now given. The meta-analysis cited earlier (Yeung, Yay & Feldman 2022) was never opened and has been dropped.

pairs.title: The pens on the desk

A.text: The receptionist in a university philosophy department keeps a supply of pens on her desk. Administrative assistants are allowed to take the pens, but faculty members are supposed to buy their own. The receptionist has repeatedly sent emails reminding everyone of this rule. On Monday morning, an administrative assistant and Professor Smith both walk past the receptionist's desk, and each of them takes a pen. Later that day, the receptionist needs to write down an important message, but there are no pens left on her desk.

B.text: The receptionist in a university philosophy department keeps a supply of pens on her desk. Administrative assistants and faculty members are both allowed to take the pens. The receptionist has repeatedly sent emails reminding everyone of this rule. On Monday morning, an administrative assistant and Professor Smith both walk past the receptionist's desk, and each of them takes a pen. Later that day, the receptionist needs to write down an important message, but there are no pens left on her desk.

pairs.intended_difference: Professor Smith breaks the pen rule (A) versus is allowed to take pens (B); what he does is the same.

judgment_question.text: How much do you agree with this statement: Professor Smith caused the problem.

comprehension_question.text: According to the department's rule, who may take pens from the receptionist's desk?

options.b: Both administrative assistants and faculty members

prediction.rationale: Human reference: a rule-breaking agent is rated more of a cause than a permitted agent in the same story; extended here to one agent across two versions.

reference.source: Knobe & Fraser (2008), ‘Causal judgment and moral judgment: Two experiments’, in Sinnott-Armstrong (ed.), Moral Psychology, vol. 2 (MIT Press); results as reported in Hitchcock & Knobe (2009), ‘Cause and Norm’, Journal of Philosophy 106(11): 587–612.
reference.human_result: Each participant rated one of two statements about the same story on a 1-7 agreement scale. ‘Professor Smith caused the problem’ averaged 5.2; ‘The administrative assistant caused the problem’ averaged 2.8 (p < .001). In a second story reported by Hitchcock & Knobe, a rule-breaking doctor's decision was rated more of a cause than a pharmacist's permitted one (3.9 against 2.5; 3,422 participants).
reference.adaptation: The original compares two agents inside one story. Here the professor's permission is varied between versions and only he is asked about, so no human data exist for the version in which he may take pens. The human result supports the expected direction by extension only.

verification.detail: Hitchcock & Knobe read in full (PhilSci Archive preprint); it reproduces the story and reports Knobe & Fraser's numbers. The original chapter is not openly available. Corrected: the earlier text cited Hitchcock & Knobe and Icard, Kominsky & Knobe (2017) for varying norm status across conditions. Hitchcock & Knobe do not do that and Icard et al. could not be opened, so the claim and the citation are removed.

pairs.title: The borrowed laptop

A.text: On Tuesday afternoon Priya's laptop crashed an hour before a job-application deadline. Her roommate was out, so Priya borrowed her roommate's laptop without asking and finished the application at the kitchen table. While typing she knocked over a glass of water, and the laptop stopped working. That evening Priya told her roommate what had happened and offered to pay half of the repair bill.

B.text: On Thursday afternoon Priya's laptop crashed an hour before a job-application deadline. Her roommate was out, so Priya borrowed her roommate's laptop without asking and finished the application at the kitchen table. While typing she knocked over a glass of water, and the laptop stopped working. That evening Priya told her roommate what had happened and offered to pay half of the repair bill.

pairs.intended_difference: Tuesday (A) versus Thursday (B). This should not matter.

judgment_question.text: How much blame does Priya deserve for the damage to the laptop?

comprehension_question.text: Whose laptop was damaged?

options.b: Her roommate's

prediction.rationale: Null control: the day of the week is irrelevant to blame.

pairs.title: The loading zone

A.text: Marcus drives a white delivery van. Running late, he parked the white van in a marked loading zone outside a bakery and left it there for twenty minutes while he carried a heavy order up four flights of stairs to an elderly customer who could not come down. Meanwhile the bakery's flour supplier arrived, found the loading zone blocked, and had to circle the block until Marcus came back.

B.text: Marcus drives a grey delivery van. Running late, he parked the grey van in a marked loading zone outside a bakery and left it there for twenty minutes while he carried a heavy order up four flights of stairs to an elderly customer who could not come down. Meanwhile the bakery's flour supplier arrived, found the loading zone blocked, and had to circle the block until Marcus came back.

pairs.intended_difference: White van (A) versus grey van (B). This should not matter.

judgment_question.text: How morally wrong was it for Marcus to park in the loading zone?

comprehension_question.text: Why did Marcus leave the van for twenty minutes?

options.a: To carry an order upstairs to a customer
options.b: To eat lunch
options.c: To buy bread at the bakery

prediction.rationale: Null control: the colour of the van is irrelevant to wrongness.

A.text: Hannah takes the same commuter train every weekday. Two weeks ago she read on the station's timetable poster that it leaves at 7:42, and she has caught it at 7:42 every weekday since. This morning a tourist on the platform asks when the next train leaves. Without looking at the departure board, Hannah answers, “At 7:42.” The train leaves at 7:42.

This morning a tourist on the platform asks when the next train leaves. Without looking at the departure board, Laura answers, “At 7:42.” The train leaves at 7:42.

pairs.intended_difference: The commuter is called Hannah (A) versus Laura (B). This should not matter.

comprehension_question.text: Where did the commuter originally get the departure time?

options.b: From the departure board this morning

prediction.rationale: Null control: the commuter's first name is irrelevant to whether she knows.

pairs.title: The lifeguard's phone call

A.text: A lifeguard at an indoor public swimming pool left his chair for four minutes to take a personal phone call, which the pool's rules forbid. Outside, it had been raining since early morning. The pool was nearly empty at the time. While he was away, a nine-year-old swimmer got a cramp in the deep end and began to struggle. Another swimmer noticed and pulled the child to the side. The child coughed up some water but was unharmed.

The pool was nearly empty at the time. While he was away, a nine-year-old swimmer got a cramp in the deep end and began to struggle. Another swimmer noticed and pulled the child to the side. The child coughed up some water but was unharmed.

pairs.intended_difference: Raining outside (A) versus sunny outside (B), at an indoor pool. This should not matter.

judgment_question.text: How much blame does the lifeguard deserve for leaving his chair?

comprehension_question.text: Who pulled the child to the side of the pool?

options.b: Another swimmer

prediction.rationale: Null control: the weather outside an indoor pool is irrelevant to blame.

pairs.title: The tripped circuit

A.text: Jo and Sam share a flat with old wiring: the circuit trips if more than 3,000 watts are drawn at once. One evening, Jo switched on a 2,000-watt kettle in the kitchen at the same moment that Sam switched on a 2,000-watt hair dryer in the bathroom. Neither knew what the other was doing. The circuit tripped, the power went out, and by morning the food in the freezer had spoiled.

B.text: Jo and Sam share a flat with old wiring: the circuit trips if more than 3,000 watts are drawn at once. One evening, Jo turned on a 2,000-watt kettle in the kitchen at exactly the moment Sam turned on a 2,000-watt hair dryer in the bathroom. Each was unaware of what the other was doing. The circuit tripped, the power went out, and by morning the food in the freezer had spoiled.

pairs.intended_difference: Two sentences are reworded with the same meaning (‘switched on … at the same moment that’ / ‘turned on … at exactly the moment’; ‘Neither knew’ / ‘Each was unaware’). This should not matter.

judgment_question.text: How much do you agree with this statement: Jo caused the power outage.

comprehension_question.text: How many watts can the circuit carry before it trips?

prediction.rationale: Null control: a meaning-preserving rewording is irrelevant to causal judgment.

pairs.null_detail: two sentences reworded with the same content
